title: China had state-issued paper money 600 years before Europe
body: In 11th-century Sichuan, merchants in Chengdu began issuing paper notes called jiaozi, because the iron coins used there were too heavy to carry in quantity. In 1023 the Song government took the idea over and opened an office to print official notes, the first state paper currency anywhere. Europe’s first banknotes came from Stockholms Banco in 1661, and they too replaced coins that were too heavy to carry: Sweden’s plate-sized copper daler. In both places the printers soon printed too much.

events.text: The Song state takes them over

left.label: Chengdu, 1023
left.text: Iron coins too heavy to carry. Paper notes stand in for them, and are later over-printed, driving up prices.

right.label: Stockholm, 1661
right.text: Plate-sized copper coins. Paper notes are easier to carry, but the bank over-issues them and stops trading within three years.

slides.label: between China’s first state banknotes and Europe’s
slides.text: From 1023 in Chengdu to 1661 in Stockholm.

slides.question: Why did Chengdu’s merchants start issuing paper notes?
options: Iron coins were too heavy to carry
slides.explanation: Sichuan used iron coins, far too heavy in quantity. Six centuries later, Stockholm’s notes replaced plate-sized copper coins for the same reason.
